newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Race debate said harming Australian tourism.
newsitem.headline: Race debate said harming Australian tourism.

text.p: Australian tourism chiefs of Monday were grappling with how best to handle the fall-out from the country's heated race debate, which has already seen several Asian tour groups cancel trips to Australia.
Australia's Tourism Task Force has called for a A$25 million (US$19 million) Asian publicity campaign to correct perceptions that Australia was returning to its racist past.

"Cancellations, coupled with a recent decline in Japanese visitors, are a cause for genuine national concern," task force chairman John Brown said in a statement. The task force is an industry association of tourism leaders.
"We need the government to reinforce the view we want Asian tourists here," Brown said. "All of that money and all of those jobs (within the tourism industry) are at threat."
The Australian tourism industry is worth around A$14 billion, with nearly four million international tourists, mainly Asian, visiting the country in 1995.
But the Tourism Council of Australia, a tourism lobby group, on Monday rejected calls for an Asian publicity campaign, arguing it would only draw attention to the race debate.

"Our main aim in terms of the issue is to stop the debate, it is the racism issue that is being reported in Asian countries which is our major concern," said Tourism Council managing director Bruce Baird.

"When you start to advertise and say we are not racist I think that draws attention to the fact, even though there's obviously some merit in being counterproductive on the issue," Baird told reporters.

Australian Tourism Minister John Moore has rejected the idea of a government-funded Asian publicity campaign, preferring to rely on the positive effects expected to flow from last week's bipartisan parliamentary motion in support of racial tolerance.
Asia accounts for 60 percent of Australia's tourists, with Japan the traditional source and Southeast Asia, Taiwan and South Korea growth areas.

A maiden parliamentary speech by independent politician Pauline Hanson on September 10 sparked Australia's race debate. Hanson called for a halt to Asian immigration, arguing incorrectly that Australia was being swamped by Asians.
Asians make up less than five percent of Australia's 18 million population and about a quarter of the annual 100,000 migrants.
The Australian Tourism Commission, the government's tourism marketing body, has reported that at least five Asian tour groups have cancelled visits to Australia since the start of the race debate.
The Commission said a group of 160 Singaporeans cancelled a visit planned for November citing "political considerations".
"We're turning against ourselves as a nation and that's damaging to our future tourism," said Commission president Jon Hutchison.
